rewritten_text:
This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper. At Lady Canterville's strong request, Mrs. Otis had agreed to keep her in her old job. She gave each of them a deep curtsy as they stepped down and said, in a charmingly old-fashioned way, “I welcome you to Canterville Chase.” They followed her through the handsome Tudor hall into the library, a long, low room lined with black oak panels, with a large stained-glass window at one end. Tea was waiting for them there. They took off their coats and wraps, sat down, and began looking around while Mrs. Umney served them.

Suddenly Mrs. Otis noticed a faded red mark on the floor beside the fireplace. Having no idea what it meant, she said to Mrs. Umney, “I'm afraid something has been spilled there.”

“Yes, madam,” the old housekeeper answered quietly. “Blood was spilled in that spot.”

“How dreadful!” Mrs. Otis cried. “I don't like bloodstains in a sitting room at all. It must be cleaned up immediately.”

The old woman smiled and replied in the same quiet, mysterious voice, “It is Lady Eleanore de Canterville's blood. Her own husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, murdered her on that very spot in 1575. Sir Simon lived nine years longer, then suddenly disappeared in very mysterious circumstances. His body has never been found, but his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. Tourists and other visitors have greatly admired the bloodstain. It cannot be removed.”

“Nonsense!” cried Washington Otis. “Pinkerton's Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clean it in no time.” Before the frightened housekeeper could stop him, he dropped to his knees and began scrubbing the floor quickly with a small stick that looked like black makeup. Within moments, every trace of the bloodstain had vanished.

“I knew Pinkerton would manage it!” he announced triumphantly, looking around at his admiring family. But he had barely finished speaking when a terrible lightning flash lit the dark room. A frightening crash of thunder brought everyone to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

“What an awful climate!” the American Minister said calmly, lighting a long cigar. “I suppose the old country is so crowded that there isn't enough decent weather for everyone. I've always thought the only answer for England is for people to move abroad.”

“My dear Hiram,” Mrs. Otis cried, “what are we to do with a woman who faints?”

“Make her pay for it, just as for breaking things,” the Minister replied. “She won't faint after that.” And sure enough, within a few moments Mrs. Umney recovered.

“Tom!”

No reply.

“TOM!”

No reply.

“Where has that boy gone? You, TOM!”

Still no reply.

The old lady lowered her glasses and looked around the room over their tops. Then she pushed them up and looked beneath them. She hardly ever looked through them for something as ordinary as a boy. They were her best pair, her pride and joy, meant to look stylish rather than help her see. She could have seen just as well through a pair of stove lids. For a moment she looked puzzled. Then she said, without anger, but loudly enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well, if I get hold of you, I'll—”

She stopped there, because she was now bending over and jabbing her broom under the bed. She needed her breath for the noises that went with each jab. All she brought out was the cat.

“I never saw another boy like him!”

She stood in the open doorway and looked among the tomato plants and jimson weeds that made up the garden. No Tom. So she raised her voice to make it carry as far as possible and shouted:

“Y-o-u-u TOM!”

A faint sound came from behind her. Turning just in time, she caught a small boy by the loose back of his short jacket and stopped his escape.

“There! I should have thought of that cupboard. What were you doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. Look at your mouth. What is that stuff?”

“I don't know, Aunt.”

“Well, I do. It's jam, that's what. I've told you forty times I'd give you a whipping if you didn't leave that jam alone. Hand me that switch.”

The thin whipping stick hung in the air. Things looked desperate—

“Oh! Look behind you, Aunt!”

The old lady spun around and pulled her skirts out of harm's way. At once the boy ran, scrambled up the tall wooden fence, and vanished over the top.

His Aunt Polly stood there in surprise for a moment, then began to laugh softly.

“That rascal! Will I never learn? Hasn't he played enough tricks like that for me to be watching out by now? But old fools are the greatest fools of all. You can't teach an old dog new tricks, as they say. Still, goodness knows, he never tries the same trick two days running. How can anyone know what's coming? He seems to know exactly how long he can bother me before I lose my temper. And he knows that if he can distract me for a minute or make me laugh, my anger disappears and I can't hit him even once.

As I put my hand through the valve with a cup of water for the old cat, my shirt-sleeves caught in the loop supporting the basket, and in an instant detached it from the bottom. Had the entire thing dissolved into air, it could not have disappeared from my view more suddenly or completely. Indeed, not a tenth of a second could have elapsed between the release of the basket and its utter disappearance, together with everything it held. I sent my good wishes after it towards the earth, but naturally entertained no hope that either the cat or her kittens would survive to relate their unhappy adventure.

“At six o'clock I noticed that a large part of the earth's visible surface to the east lay beneath a dense shadow. This moved forward with remarkable speed, until, at five minutes to seven, night covered the whole expanse before me. Yet the light of the setting sun continued to shine upon the balloon until long afterwards; and although I had, of course, expected this, the circumstance afforded me a very great pleasure. Plainly, in the morning I should see the sun rise at least several hours before the inhabitants of Rotterdam, despite their position so much farther east. Thus, with every day, and in proportion to my increasing elevation, I should enjoy sunlight for a longer and longer interval. I resolved now to maintain a journal of my voyage, counting each day continuously from one hour to twenty-four, without regard to periods of darkness.

“At ten o'clock, growing drowsy, I decided to lie down for the remainder of the night. Here, however, a difficulty arose which, obvious though it may seem, had entirely escaped me until the moment I describe. If I slept as intended, how was the air within the chamber to be renewed meanwhile? It would be impossible to breathe it for longer than an hour at most; and even if that time could be stretched to an hour and a quarter, the most disastrous effects might follow. This predicament occasioned me considerable uneasiness. It will scarcely be credited that, after all the dangers I had already encountered, I regarded this problem so gravely as to abandon every hope of achieving my ultimate purpose, and at last to conclude that I must descend. My uncertainty, however, endured only for a moment.
